summary:
Nimrod Hauser introduces the challenge of using third-party agentic tools in production AI applications. These tools are callable functions wrapped with descriptions that guide agents on when and how to use them, but external authors cannot anticipate every consumer's architecture. The talk focuses on Playwright's MCP server, which provides 21 browser-manipulation tools with intentionally generic descriptions.

Baz's spec reviewer serves as the concrete use case: an agentic QA tool that reads requirements from ticketing systems and Figma designs, then uses Playwright's MCP server to verify implementations and produce pass/fail verdicts with screenshot evidence. The baseline V0 run using unmodified LangChain load MCP tools fails—the agent hallucinates a URL, returns a false-negative verdict, and captures a broken 404 screenshot.

Hauser presents five best practices, organized into context engineering and deterministic guardrails buckets. First, curating third-party tools: excluding unnecessary tools like browser resizing, dragging, and code execution, reducing 21 tools to 16. Second, wrapping tools with custom descriptions tailored to the use case—for example, instructing the agent to call the accessibility snapshot tool before hover or click actions. Third, adding deterministic guardrails for sensitive operations: the screenshot path validation prevents storage outside a designated folder and returns agent-friendly error messages guiding the agent to retry with a correct path rather than crashing the flow. Fourth, creating composite tools from existing ones: an evidence-specific screenshot tool with a specialized description instructing the agent to include the ticket number in the filename, allowing the agent to differentiate between general screenshots and evidence captures. Fifth, treating tools as plain deterministic functions outside the agentic flow: the login_to_buzz function deterministically injects JWT tokens into browser local storage before the agent starts, removing login complexity from the agent's context. The final V5 run succeeds: the agent correctly identifies the configuration drawer as present, captures a properly named screenshot, and returns a passing verdict. Hauser notes pixel-perfect verification was achieved in the real product but omitted from the toy example. The framework emphasizes iteratively molding tools to best fit each use case, balancing curation against verbose descriptions and deterministic control against agentic flexibility.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Third-party agentic tools rarely work optimally out of the box because their authors cannot anticipate your specific architecture or use case
Curating tools by excluding unnecessary ones reduces context window size and simplifies agent tool selection—Playwright's 21 tools reduced to 16
Wrapping tools with custom descriptions lets you inject domain-specific guidance, such as instructing agents to call accessibility snapshots before click or hover actions

Composite tools built from existing ones allow specialized behavior for specific contexts, like an evidence-screenshot tool that includes ticket numbers in filenames
Treating MCP tools as plain deterministic functions outside the agentic flow simplifies mandatory actions like login by removing them from agent context
The framework balances context engineering (curating, wrapping, composites) with deterministic enforcement (guardrails, plain functions) to make MCP integrations production-ready
Iterative tool molding requires balancing curation against verbose descriptions and deterministic control against agentic flexibility—there is no one-size-fits-all

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Hauser introduces himself as a founding engineer at Baz, which builds AI-powered code review agents. He frames the talk around fixing a broken MCP server and outlines the agenda: understanding why third-party tools fail, exploring five best practices, and iteratively improving a busted MCP server.

sections.title: Third-Party Agentic Tools: Challenges and Risks
sections.summary: Defines third-party agentic tools as callable functions wrapped with descriptions, regardless of source (MCP, library, copy-paste). Explains they can cause unexpected agent behavior, performance degradation, and security issues like multi-tenant data leaks. Introduces Playwright's MCP server as the running example.

sections.title: Use Case: Baz Spec Reviewer
sections.summary: Describes the spec reviewer product: an agentic QA tool that reads requirements from ticketing systems and Figma designs, then uses Playwright's MCP server to verify implementations and produce pass/fail verdicts with screenshot evidence, automating PM validation work.

sections.title: Code Walkthrough and Baseline Configuration
sections.summary: Walks through the toy spec reviewer code: MCP client configuration with Playwright, a base class with get_tools method for iterative improvement, system and human prompts with multimodal image embedding, and the V0 baseline using LangChain's unmodified load MCP tools.

sections.title: V0 Baseline Run and Failure Analysis
sections.summary: Runs the baseline V0 with 21 unmodified Playwright tools. The agent fails: it hallucinates a URL (buzz.co/spec-reviewer), returns a false-negative 'not implemented' verdict, and captures a broken 404 screenshot. This failure demonstrates the core problem the talk addresses.

sections.title: Five Best Practices Overview
sections.summary: Introduces the five concepts: curating third-party tools, wrapping tools with custom descriptions, adding deterministic guardrails, creating new composite tools from existing ones, and treating tools as plain functions outside the agentic flow. Organizes them into context engineering and deterministic guardrails buckets.

sections.title: V1 Curated: Excluding Unnecessary Tools
sections.summary: Demonstrates V1 curated: filtering out 6 unnecessary Playwright tools (resize, drag, code execution) using a Python list comprehension, reducing 21 tools to 16. This shrinks the context window and simplifies agent tool selection, though some later practices will add context back.

sections.title: V2 Wrapped: Custom Tool Descriptions
sections.summary: Demonstrates V2 wrapped: creating a tool wrapper class that maps tool names to enhanced descriptions. Key example: instructing the agent to call the accessibility snapshot tool before hover or click, and to prefer accessibility snapshots over visual snapshots. The wrapper creates new tool objects invoking original tools with enhanced descriptions.

sections.title: V3 Guardrails: Deterministic Path Validation
sections.summary: Demonstrates V3 guardrails: adding a path validation class that deterministically validates screenshot storage paths against a designated screenshots root folder before invocation. Invalid paths raise an error but return agent-friendly messages explaining where to save, allowing the agent to retry aligned rather than crashing the agentic flow. Motivated by agents being non-deterministic and potentially ignoring prompt instructions.

sections.title: V4 Composite: Evidence-Specific Screenshot Tool
sections.summary: Demonstrates V4 composite tools: injecting a new evidence-specific screenshot tool built on the existing screenshot tool. The tool has a specialized description instructing the agent to use it only for evidence capture and to include the ticket number in the saved filename. This allows the agent to differentiate between general screenshots and evidence captures, with the option to add tool-specific guardrails or deterministic actions.

sections.title: V5 Deterministic Functions: Login Outside Agentic Flow
sections.summary: Demonstrates V5: calling the login_to_buzz function deterministically before agent creation. The function plucks relevant MCP tools, injects JWT tokens from environment variables into browser local storage, and logs in without agent involvement. Rationale: login is mandatory, complex, involves secrets, and varies per client—giving subpar results when left to the agent. This unburdens the agent's context from clunky mandatory actions.

sections.title: Final Run and Summary
sections.summary: Runs the fully improved V5: the agent logs in via JWT, navigates to the correct page, finds the configuration drawer, returns a correct passing verdict, and captures a properly named screenshot including the ticket number. Hauser notes pixel-perfect verification works in the real product but was omitted from this toy example. Concludes with a summary emphasizing that tools must be iteratively molded—balancing curation versus verbose descriptions and deterministic control versus agentic flexibility—with no one-size-fits-all approach.

demonstrations: Toy example of Baz's spec reviewer using Playwright MCP server to verify a configuration drawer feature against a ticket and Figma design
